extracted.intended_audience: readers of classic literature / general readers of Cervantes (curate and barber characters debating book merits)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and reasons used by the curate, barber, housekeeper and niece to decide which books to burn, preserve, expurgate, or banish — focused on books of chivalry, romances, and poetry in a household library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books_of_chivalry_cause_mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: “these accursed books of chivalry… have upset his reason;” the curate and housekeeper present books of chivalry as harmful influences that lead readers to madness or dangerous behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basis for wholesale condemnation/burning: if a book belongs to the chivalry-romance genre it is presumed capable of doing real mischief (making the uncle behave as a knight-errant) and therefore is a candidate for destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine_titles_before_condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate directs the barber to give him the books one by one to see what they were about before deciding which to burn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not condemn an entire library blindly; inspect titles/contents and make individual judgements rather than indiscriminate punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder_or_early_work_bears_special_blame
rubrics_metrics.description: On finding 'The four books of Amadis of Gaul' the curate says it 'was the first book of chivalry printed in Spain, and from this all the others derive their birth and origin; so it seems to me that we ought inexorably to condemn it to the flames as the founder of so vile a sect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign extra responsibility to seminal works: early/foundational texts that spawned a harmful genre are judged more culpable and targeted for destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit_within_genre_may_excuse_punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The barber: 'this is the best of all the books of this kind that have been written, and so... it ought to be pardoned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even within a problematic genre, books showing distinguishable quality or merit can be spared; evaluate intrinsic literary quality when deciding fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style_quality_as_ground_for_condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate condemns certain works 'for the stiffness and dryness of his style [which] deserve nothing else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic failings (stiffness, dryness, awkwardness) are cited as reasons to condemn or burn a book; aesthetic style matters in the verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious_or_symbolic_content_suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Of 'The Knight of the Cross' the curate says 'For the sake of the holy name this book has its ignorance might be excused; but then, they say, "behind the cross there’s the devil;" to the fire with it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works invoking religious symbols can be double-edged: pious titles do not guarantee safety—suspicious or ignorant religious usage may prompt condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation_quality_and_original_language_consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate complains that translating verse 'robbed him of a great deal of his natural force' and that translators 'never can reach the level of the originals as they were first produced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations are viewed skeptically; books in translation may be judged inferior or be treated differently than originals, and works kept in original language may be spared from condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author_reputation_and_provenance_matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate spares 'Palmerin of England' and praises it because 'it is said to have been written by a wise and witty king of Portugal' and because 'language is polished and clear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial reputation, provenance, and claimed authorship influence decisions—works by admired or notable authors receive more lenient treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot_contrivance_and_inventive_adventures_as_positive_criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: 'All the adventures at the Castle of Miraguarda are excellent and of admirable contrivance,' cited as reasons to preserve a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive plotting and well-contrived adventures are positive literary qualities that weigh in favour of preservation rather than destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre_distinction:_poetry_vs_chivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate: 'these must be, not chivalry, but poetry… these do not deserve to be burned like the others, for they neither do nor can do the mischief the books of chivalry have done, being books of entertainment that can hurt no one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres are judged by different risks: poetry and certain prose entertainment are considered less dangerous than chivalric romances and thus are more likely to be preserved (or only lightly censored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential_to_influence_reader_behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The niece argues that reading poetry could lead the uncle to 'turn shepherd' or 'turn poet,' which she considers 'an incurable and infectious malady.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge books on the likelihood they will change readers' behaviour or life choices; works that might produce eccentric or socially undesirable emulation are treated more harshly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expurgation_and_editing_as_alternative_to_burning
rubrics_metrics.description: The curate proposes the 'Diana' 'should not be burned, but that it should be cleared of all that about the sage Felicia and the magic water, and of almost all the longer pieces of verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than total destruction, excise objectionable passages (magic, superstitious elements, long verse) to render a book acceptable—editing/expurgation is a viable remedial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delightfulness_and_singularity_as_positive_qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Of 'The Fortune of Love' the curate says 'so droll and absurd a book as this has never been written, and in its way it is the best and the most singular of all of this species... delightful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality, singular charm and the capacity to delight readers are cited as admirable traits that recommend a book for preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weeding_vulgarities_and_preservation_for_personal_connections
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This book must be weeded and cleansed of certain vulgarities which it has with its excellences; let it be preserved because the author is a friend of mine,' the curate says of a poems collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove vulgar or coarse elements to salvage a work's merits; personal relationships and patronage can sway decisions, though the stated substantive reason is to expurgate vulgarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic_human_detail_and_everyday_knightly_life_are_valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: About 'Tirante el Blanco' the curate calls it 'a treasury of enjoyment and a mine of recreation... Here knights eat and sleep, and die in their beds,' praising its realistic, domestic depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary representations that show humanizing, believable detail (knights' everyday life, wills before dying) are counted as virtues distinguishing a valuable book within the genre.
